articles.title: Grassley under the gun over hidden docs behind botched attack on Jack Smith
articles.description: Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-IA) is under fire from Democrats for hiding documents related to former special counsel Jack Smith that led to Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-MO) embarrassing himself in a recent nationally televised hearing. A letter led by ranking member Dick Durbin (D-IL), obtained by Politico, centers on Schmitt, who at a hearing last month suggested Smith secretly attended an NBA game in Atlanta on Feb. 3, 2024, to meet with prosecutors working on the Georgia election case against President Donald Trump. Schmitt displayed a giant poster of text messages from Smith’s team to make his case. Smith denied it and Democrats say the texts “established only that Senator Schmitt had not done the basic due diligence of verifying a document before relying on it.” The episode, the Democrats wrote, “caused needless confusion, slowed down the business of the Committee, introduced the possibility that false information would be entered uncontested into the record, and created an embarrassing stain on one of the most important committees in Congress.” Democrats say they didn’t get the materials Schmitt used ahead of the hearing, so they were “forced to synthesize these baseless accusations and respond in real time," Politico reported. They also pointed to another record they say wasn’t shared in advance: a readout of an Aug. 17, 2024, call between Smith and the Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section, which Schmitt and fellow Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley both cited at the hearing. “We ask that you immediately provide all committee records that you have withheld, commit to fully complying with Senate Rules … going forward, and apologize to Mr. Smith on behalf of the Committee,” the Democrats wrote. Grassley spokesperson Clare Slattery responded in a statement: “it’s Jack Smith who owes an apology to the thousands of Americans he and his staff ran roughshod over.”

articles.title: 'Warning shot' fired at White House over ex-official who waltzed into oil industry job
articles.description: California Democrats are demanding answers from a former White House energy adviser who went to work for an oil company she had helped while in government. Sens. Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla and Rep. Salud Carbajal sent a letter Wednesday to Brittany Kelm seeking answers about her tenure as a senior adviser on the National Energy Dominance Council, where part of her portfolio was helping Sable Offshore Corp. restart production on its oil platforms off the coast of Santa Barbara, reported Politico . Kelm left the White House in August to become vice president of policy and commercial at Sable, whose platforms have been opposed by California officials since an oil spill in the area. "Your new role, considering your prior close relationship with Sable while serving as a White House Senior Policy Adviser for Oil and Gas, raises serious questions about your compliance with federal ethics laws," the lawmakers wrote. The letter cites public comments from Kelm and other administration officials promoting Sable while she was in government. It also points to an instance in which a Sable executive credited Kelm's efforts to help the company. The lawmakers asked Kelm to preserve all records and communications related to Sable and to answer a series of questions about her dealings with the company. The inquiry is the latest "warning shot" from Democrats previewing the oversight investigations they could launch if they win control of Congress in November, according to Politico. Democrats have also signaled interest in the Trump administration's oil projects in Venezuela and its critical minerals deals. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers brushed off the letter, saying California Democrats "will do anything but address the massive problems plaguing their state." She insisted that Kelm followed all ethics rules. "As is standard practice in every administration, White House employees coordinate their departures with ethics officials to ensure full compliance with all applicable guidelines and restrictions during offboarding," Rogers said. Kelm and Sable did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The dispute is part of a larger fight between the administration and California. After the state blocked Sable from restarting a pipeline idled by a major oil leak, the company turned to the Trump administration for help. In March, the Energy Department invoked the Defense Production Act to order the pipeline restarted. Gov. Gavin Newsom has called the move illegal, and the state is fighting it in court.
